title: Which Sugar Sits Where
endLine: On the cell surface, the message is which sugar sits where.

scenes.tts: The first film followed one glucose bond, whose face decides fuel or fiber. Now look at a red blood cell. Short sugar chains bristle from its surface. Change one small sugar at their tips, and it changes which blood you can receive. How can one sugar matter that much?
scenes.visual: CARRY FILM 1'S WORLD AND COLOUR MAP: glucose TILES (rounded squares 1.3 wide, white fill 15%, WHITE outline) with the TEAL 'C6' tab on top, GOLD pin on the right edge (the anomeric carbon) and WHITE port '4'; GOLD = the anomeric carbon and its bond; TEAL = carbon six; BLUE alpha, GREEN beta (only if a bond face is shown); RED = 'cannot' marks only; PURPLE = proteins that act on or read sugars (enzymes, lectins, hemagglutinin). NEW IN THIS FILM: the CELL SURFACE, a horizontal membrane drawn as two WHITE parallel lines across the lower quarter of the frame (y -2.4 and -2.8, x -6.2..6.2) with a slow ripple (updater). Short SUGAR STALKS rise from it: each a vertical chain of 3 to 4 small tiles (0.6 wide) joined by small GOLD joints, swaying gently (amplitude 0.05, period 3 s). New sugar identities are tile fills at 70%: ORANGE 'A sugar', PINK 'B sugar', MAGENTA 'sialic acid' (with a small minus badge). Chain lengths and sugar counts are 'schematic' (TEXT 28, bottom-right, whenever stalks are shown). Labels 30+, full opacity, at most 5 words; at most 6 things on screen. No molecular structures anywhere: tiles, tabs, pins, chips and cartoons only. SCENE: NO fade from black. Open on film 1's last picture: two glucose tiles at frame centre joined by the GOLD joint, its flag rocking between the BLUE (down) and GREEN (up) faces; tiny cartoon bread (BLUE outline) left and plank (GREEN outline) right at 40%. On 'fuel or fiber' bread and plank fade out and the two tiles shrink and rise into place as the top of one sugar stalk. On 'a red blood cell' the camera pulls back: a large cartoon red-cell disc (MAROON outline, not RED, filling 60% of frame height) whose lower rim flattens into the membrane of the world; eight sugar stalks stand along it, swaying. On 'at their tips' the tip tile of each stalk pulses WHITE. On 'Change one small sugar' the tip of the centre stalk swaps from a WHITE tile to an ORANGE tile and back. On 'which blood you can receive' a small cartoon blood bag (WHITE outline) slides in at upper right, then a second bag beside it gets a RED X (40). On 'How can one sugar' everything dims to 40% except the one ORANGE tip tile, which glows.
scenes.narration: The first film followed one glucose bond, whose face decides fuel or fiber. Now look at a red blood cell. Short sugar chains bristle from its surface. Change one small sugar at their tips, and it changes which blood you can receive. How can one sugar matter that much?

scenes.visual: Do not cut away: the stalks keep swaying at 30% opacity and the ORANGE tip keeps a soft glow. Over them: the title 'Which Sugar Sits Where' (TITLE_FONT 54) and a GOLD rule. Title out in the last 0.4 s; the blood bags slide away and the red-cell outline fades, leaving the membrane and its stalks filling the lower 60% of the frame.

scenes.tts: Most proteins on a cell's surface, and most it secretes, carry chains like these. Every link in them still runs through an anomeric carbon. So the first rule tells you where each link is. It cannot tell you what the coat says.
scenes.visual: Membrane and stalks fill the frame. On 'Most proteins' four PURPLE rounded blobs labelled 'protein' (30, one label only) rise from the membrane under four of the stalks, so the stalks now hang from proteins; on 'and most it secretes' one protein with its stalk detaches and drifts up and out of frame at upper left. On 'Every link' the camera eases in on one stalk until it fills 60% of frame height; each GOLD joint between its tiles flashes in turn from base to tip, with one label 'anomeric carbon' (GOLD, 30). On 'where each link is' small GOLD dots mark every joint and stay. On 'what the coat says' the tiles themselves get a WHITE question mark (40) beside the stalk, while the GOLD dots stay lit.
scenes.narration: Most proteins on a cell's surface, and most it secretes, carry chains like these. Every link in them still runs through an anomeric carbon. So the first rule tells you where each link is. It cannot tell you what the coat says.

scenes.tts: Your blood type shows what it says. Red cells carry a shared core chain, called the H antigen. Which sugar lands on its tip depends on the enzyme you inherit.
scenes.visual: The stalk returns to its place; three identical stalks now stand side by side on the membrane at x -4, 0 and 4, each 50% of frame height, swaying. On 'shared core chain' all three stalks glow WHITE together and a bracket labelled 'H antigen' (30) spans one of them. On 'lands on its tip' an empty dashed tile outline appears on top of each stalk. On 'the enzyme you inherit' three small PURPLE enzyme cartoons (pac-man shapes, as in film 1) drop in above the three stalks, labelled 'A enzyme', 'B enzyme', 'O allele' (30 each).
scenes.narration: Your blood type shows what it says. Red cells carry a shared core chain, called the H antigen. Which sugar lands on its tip depends on the enzyme you inherit.

scenes.tts: The A enzyme adds one sugar. The B enzyme adds a different one, by the same bond. The O allele adds nothing at all.
scenes.visual: On 'The A enzyme adds' the left enzyme carries an ORANGE tile down and clicks it onto the left stalk's tip through a GOLD joint; label 'type A' (ORANGE, 32) under that stalk. On 'The B enzyme' the middle enzyme clicks a PINK tile onto the middle tip; label 'type B' (PINK, 32). On 'by the same bond' the two new GOLD joints flash together. On 'adds nothing' the right 'O allele' cartoon fades to an empty outline and carries nothing; the right tip stays bare; label 'type O' (WHITE, 32). The enzyme cartoons then fade out.
scenes.narration: The A enzyme adds one sugar. The B enzyme adds a different one, by the same bond. The O allele adds nothing at all.

scenes.tts: And the A and B sugars differ at only one carbon, carbon two. One small difference at the tip sets your blood type.
scenes.visual: The ORANGE and PINK tip tiles lift off their stalks (ghosts stay in place) and enlarge side by side at upper centre, each 30% of frame height, same tile shape. Each carries one small badge on its edge marked 'C2'. On 'only one carbon' the two C2 badges blink: on the ORANGE tile the badge is a larger WHITE square, on the PINK tile a small WHITE dot; every other part of the two tiles is identical and pulses together. On 'sets your blood type' the two tiles drop back onto their stalks and the 'type A' and 'type B' labels pulse once.
scenes.narration: And the A and B sugars differ at only one carbon, carbon two. One small difference at the tip sets your blood type.

scenes.tts: That is the second rule. On the cell surface, what a protein reads is which sugar, joined by which bond, at which position.
scenes.visual: The three stalks (A, B, O) stay at 70%. Across the top a GOLD rule draws and three chips appear left to right on the words: 'which sugar' (WHITE, 32) as the ORANGE and PINK tips glow; 'which bond' (GOLD, 32) as their GOLD tip joints glow; 'which position' (TEAL, 32) as a short TEAL arrow points to the tip end of a stalk. The three chips stay for the next scene, side by side, at 30 size.
scenes.narration: That is the second rule. On the cell surface, what a protein reads is which sugar, joined by which bond, at which position.

scenes.tts: The cell writes addresses this way too. A mannose six phosphate tag sends enzymes to the lysosome. Lose the ability to write that tag, and the enzymes are dumped into the blood instead. That is I-cell disease.
scenes.caption: The cell writes addresses this way too. A mannose-6-phosphate tag sends enzymes to the lysosome. Lose the ability to write that tag, and the enzymes are dumped into the blood instead. That is I-cell disease.
scenes.visual: The membrane and stalks slide down to a thin strip at the bottom. Above, a cartoon cell interior: a round lysosome bubble (WHITE outline, label 'lysosome', 30) at upper left, and an exit gap in the membrane at right with an arrow labelled 'blood' (30). On 'A mannose six phosphate tag' a PURPLE enzyme blob carrying a short stalk appears at centre; its tip tile's TEAL C6 tab lights up with a small TEAL badge 'P'; one label 'mannose-6-phosphate tag' (TEAL, 30). On 'sends enzymes to the lysosome' three tagged enzyme blobs glide into the lysosome. On 'Lose the ability' the TEAL badges fade off the next three blobs (a RED X, 40, flashes over a tag); on 'dumped into the blood' those untagged blobs drift past the lysosome and out through the gap toward 'blood'. On 'I-cell disease' a chip 'I-cell disease' (RED, 30) appears by the gap.
scenes.narration: The cell writes addresses this way too. A mannose-6-phosphate tag sends enzymes to the lysosome. Lose the ability to write that tag, and the enzymes are dumped into the blood instead. That is I-cell disease.

scenes.tts: A code needs readers. Here the readers are lectins, proteins that bind specific sugar chains. But any single sugar grip is weak.
scenes.visual: Back to the cell surface filling the lower 60% of the frame, eight stalks swaying, their tips a mix of ORANGE, PINK and MAGENTA tiles. On 'readers' a PURPLE lectin (a rounded cap with one notched pocket on its underside, 2 units wide) floats down from above; label 'lectin' (PURPLE, 30). On 'bind specific sugar chains' its pocket settles onto one tip whose shape fits. On 'grip is weak' the lectin wobbles and lifts off again, settles, lifts off again: a looping on-off, with a thin dotted line marking its single contact.
scenes.narration: A code needs readers. Here the readers are lectins, proteins that bind specific sugar chains. But any single sugar grip is weak.

scenes.tts: So how can a lectin hold on firmly enough to matter? Picture an answer before you hear one.
scenes.visual: The lectin keeps flickering on and off its one tip. On 'firmly enough' a question card 'How to hold on?' (TEXT, 40) drops into the upper centre and stays.
scenes.narration: So how can a lectin hold on firmly enough to matter? Picture an answer before you hear one.

scenes.visual: Near-silence. The card 'How to hold on?' stays. The lectin keeps landing and lifting off its single tip; stalks keep swaying; a thin GOLD progress ring around the card fills over 4.5 s. Nothing else changes.

scenes.tts: It grips many sugars at once. Many weak handholds add up to a strong, selective grip. Think of hook and loop tape: no single hook would hold.
scenes.visual: The card lifts away. On 'many sugars at once' the lectin widens into a long PURPLE bar with five notched pockets along its underside and settles onto five neighbouring tips at once; five dotted contact lines light. On 'weak handholds' the contacts flicker independently, one or two letting go at a time, while the bar stays down. On 'strong, selective grip' the bar holds still while its contacts keep flickering. On 'hook and loop' a small inset at upper right: a cartoon strip of tiny hooks meeting tiny loops (WHITE outlines); on 'no single hook' one hook alone pops free while the strip as a whole stays shut.
scenes.narration: It grips many sugars at once. Many weak handholds add up to a strong, selective grip. Think of hook and loop tape: no single hook would hold.

scenes.tts: Selectins, one lectin family, use this trick. Their many grips slow circulating immune cells at a site of injury.
scenes.visual: The surface rotates into a horizontal vessel wall along the bottom of the frame (same membrane and stalks), with a slow left-to-right flow of pale dots above it. A round immune cell (WHITE outline, label 'immune cell', 30) rolls in from the left fast; on 'Selectins' PURPLE many-pocket bars on the wall light up, label 'selectins' (PURPLE, 30). On 'slow circulating immune cells' each touch between the cell and the wall drags on it, and it rolls more slowly with each contact. On 'site of injury' a small WHITE spark icon (not RED) marks the wall ahead and the cell rolls slowly to a near stop beside it.
scenes.narration: Selectins, one lectin family, use this trick. Their many grips slow circulating immune cells at a site of injury.

scenes.tts: The flu virus reads the same code. Its hemagglutinin is a lectin. It grips sialic acid, the charged sugar capping chains on your airway cells. That grip is how the virus latches on before it gets in.
scenes.visual: Back to the surface, relabelled 'airway cell' (30); every stalk now ends in a MAGENTA tip tile with a small minus badge, label 'sialic acid' (MAGENTA, 30) on one. On 'The flu virus' a round virus cartoon (WHITE outline, 1.8 units wide) drifts in from upper right, studded with short PURPLE spikes; on 'hemagglutinin' one spike glows with label 'hemagglutinin' (PURPLE, 30). On 'grips sialic acid' three spikes dock onto three MAGENTA tips at once; dotted contact lines light. On 'latches on' the virus stops drifting and sits on the surface; on 'before it gets in' the membrane begins to dimple slightly under it (schematic).
scenes.narration: The flu virus reads the same code. Its hemagglutinin is a lectin. It grips sialic acid, the charged sugar capping chains on your airway cells. That grip is how the virus latches on before it gets in.

scenes.tts: So one small sugar matters because the coat is read like a message. The readers, ours or a virus's, care which sugar sits where.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the opening picture: the red-cell disc (MAROON outline) with its eight stalks, the A, B and O tips now visible along it. On 'one small sugar' the ORANGE tip from the hook glows again. On 'read like a message' a PURPLE many-pocket lectin bar sweeps slowly along the row of tips, touching each one, and the tips light in turn as it passes. On 'which sugar sits where' the three chips from s06 'which sugar', 'which bond', 'which position' reappear above the cell in a row and stay.
scenes.narration: So one small sugar matters because the coat is read like a message. The readers, ours or a virus's, care which sugar sits where.

scenes.visual: EndCard. LINE: 'On the cell surface, the message is which sugar sits where.' Above the line, one small sugar stalk sways with its ORANGE tip glowing and its GOLD joints lit.
